utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we have the case called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, you may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Andrew Cayley, assisted by case manager Denise Gustin. Good afternoon Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Marela Jevtovic on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I am Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic. I represent General Talic together with Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I have an explanation for the absence from the courtroom of Maitre de Roux.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I presented his excuses yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was for yesterday. And for today?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the presence is requested of either the lead counsel or co-counsel, not of both counsel at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are wrong, Madam Fauveau. You should consult with the office that the presence of both of you is required, and that only occasionally and for really good reasons should either of you not be excused from being present. General Talic, were you informed that Maitre de Roux would not be present today? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I was informed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is no doubt aware of the -- or Your Honours are no doubt aware of the events that transpired this morning during the conference held under Rule 65 ter with your senior legal officer. And the motion which was filed this morning jointly on behalf of both accused. Your Honour, we received literally a minute before I came into court an order regarding the trial scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We haven't even seen it, actually. We know that it has been handed and that it was handed to you, and it was in the hands of the senior legal officer. But I haven't seen it. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number really of different matters which arise. The first is, it is my view that the filing of this motion arises as a result of not just one but a number of misunderstandings, really arising from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may I stop you for the time being, because you are preempting something that we had in mind of clarifying, and that is that before the commencement of this sitting -- today's sitting, apart from the decision by Judge Schomburg that I have just read, namely that on a provisional basis, it is being decided that the proceedings may go on until further order, and the requirement of the parties to be present today at 2.15. We had agreed amongst the -- amongst us to make a statement in open court today because we feel -- we consider this to be on importance. And the statement is as follows: -- It's a joint statement, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just interrupt before Your Honour -- and I think Mr. Ackerman is going to say the same thing. I think one of the problems is going to be that -- I'm not sure if either one or both accused have not been fully been put in the picture. And I think before Your Honours perhaps make a statement, an opportunity ought to be given. I believe it applies mainly to Mr. Brdjanin, but maybe also to General Talic. And I see Mr. Ackerman is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to request 20 minutes to confer with my client, Your Honour, before you make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 20 minutes break. --- Break taken at 2.23 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to say anything, either Ms. Korner or Mr. Ackerman or whoever?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think perhaps it -- if Your Honours have prepared a statement to make, if Your Honours were to make it and then thereafter we see where we go from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we have -- the three Judges have met on the matter arising out of the filing of the motion this morning, and we have agreed to make the following joint declaration to be entered into the records of this case. The three Judges composing this Trial Chamber in view of the joint motion of the accused filed earlier today seeking to disqualify the Trial Chamber hearing this case wish to make the following formal statement. The motion appears to be mainly based on the statement contained in the document given to the parties entitled "List of potentially agreed facts," to which the motion refers as being a list which the Chamber itself has drafted. The three Judges wish to state that the motion is obviously based on a misconception, in that none of us, the three Judges in this Trial, had anything to do with the compilation, let alone the drafting of the list of possible agreed facts for consideration. In fact, none of us, the three Judges, had even seen the said list before the present motion was filed. Having made this formal statement, the Trial Chamber wishes to state that it expects the parties to accept the assurance given by us, the three Judges composing it, namely -- I repeat that we had nothing to do with the compilation and the drafting of the so-called list of potentially agreed facts they have objections to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say straight away this is something that I had certainly gathered and expressed shortly when the matter was raised in the conference held this morning. Your Honours, it's perfectly clear, from the way it was drafted, because it contained an obvious error of fact in the first statement, in that it suggested that a letter had been sent ex parte to the Prosecution on the 28th of February, when in fact -- and I have the document here, and I believe it's now accepted by Mr. Ackerman, it was a letter sent to all parties in respect of, it was hoped, agreements which could be reached. Your Honours -- Your Honours, one can see it's addressed to myself and Mr. Cayley and Ms. Maglov and Mr. Ackerman and Mr. De Roux and Madame Fauveau, and it effectively sets out what I think anyone can see is the intention of the Trial Chamber to try and move matters along in the most efficient way that one can. Unfortunately, what appears to have happened is this, that whoever drafted this particular list of potentially agreed facts, A, said that the Chamber had drafted it, which led, I believe, Defence counsel to believe that Your Honours had drafted it; and secondly, contained an attempt to reach agreement on a fact that clearly was never going to be agreed but from the beginning of this case has been clearly the subject of contention, namely that General Talic was a member of the ARK Crisis Staff. Your Honour, that's what I say, this has been arisen from a series of misunderstandings. And because I know that neither accused comes from a system where this type of document is produced during the course of a trial, I would like to try and explain, even though I know that Your Honours know it, so that the accused hear what we've said. And it's something that we've mentioned before in court. This case concerns the alleged responsibility of a general and a senior politician for events through what the Prosecution allege is their authority at the time. It is not suggested, save for odd meetings and matters that we, for instance, dealt with yesterday, when General Talic went to Sanski Most on the 20th of April, that either accused took part in actual killings or beatings or any of the sorts. The Prosecution case is that they were ultimately criminally liable -- that's the allegation we make because of their position. The -- both accused, as Mr. Brdjanin made clear the other day, have been waiting through no fault of theirs or anyone's really, because of court scheduling, a long time for their trial. In order to make that trial efficient and for the accused to be able to best ask Your Honours to concentrate on what is relevant, as happens in trials conducted in such a system all over the world, is that facts which are not disputed as opposed to agreed, because that the accused know they happened, but simply that because the accused were not present, they cannot know one way or another whether such events took place, and it is perhaps as we discussed in the original conference with Mr. Von Hebel and Defence counsel at which the accused were not present, there was a discussion about that very matter. And Your Honours, I'm sorry I haven't got copies, but I have brought here with me the record that was made -- the official transcript of that conference when this matter was discussed. And it was raised in connection with the length of trial and the number of witnesses that would be called, and it was raised by me that where witnesses were not going to name either of the accused if the Defence could indicate what parts will be in dispute and what will not be in dispute. There was then -- Mr. Von Hebel at the end of my request that we told what was not going to be disputed said this: "Are there any comments from either Defence counsel?" And Mr. De Roux said: "Yes. I think that I personally can't agree because the Prosecution want to establish a number of facts. That's the Prosecution." It's quite difficult to follow what he said. But anyhow, he said: "I think there are a number of facts that of course we can discuss." Mr. Ackerman was asked for his opinion and pointed out that with two defendants, it was quite difficult to reach agreement. He said: "One defendant may be willing to agree to a whole list of facts that happened. And another defendant may want to agree to a third of them.." Then he said this: "I think as time goes by, some of these things will be taken care of." And then Mr. Von Hebel went on and explained that there might be -- before we got into the next municipality, where there are certain facts which probably do not implicate the accused themselves, if we can agree amongst the parties to those fact, I would again invite the Prosecution in this respect for the municipality to try and elaborate a list maybe based on one which was submitted at sometime ago." And then Mr. De Roux said this: "There were a number of facts of which the Defence has absolutely no knowledge, so we cannot admit or accept the list of facts of which we have absolutely no knowledge." And then we had this discussion about producing a list, with facts that the Defence cannot dispute. The matter rested there but has been raised on a number of occasions and in particular when the -- Your Honours raised it, in fact, at the next hearing on the 18th of February. Your Honour Judge Agius said: "Agreed facts --" can I say this is the bottom -- this is the transcript page 1883. And you talked about the possibility -- possibly also with the help of our senior legal officer to try at least identify various facts on which there should be no reason for you to disagree about." And both accused were present to hear that being said. And you gave various examples. And Mr. Ackerman, in response, said this: -- There had been a discussion about it, and it was difficult because of the representation of General Talic at that stage undergoing some kind of flux. And he said that at the bottom of page 1887: "It will be of absolutely no value at this point or perhaps any time in the future for us to have some kind of a meeting with the Prosecutor, because we know what the facts are that are alleged by the Prosecutor, and we are perfectly capable, the two Defence teams I hope, of sitting down and saying we should go along with some of these. Now, one thing they might ask the Chamber to consider which might make this an easier process, rather than for us to say to the Trial Chamber, "We admit this certain set of facts," is if we could be permitted to say to the Trial Chamber that we do not contest this particular set of facts."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all the facts with regard to what happened at the camp at Omarska, and another thing to say, we simply do not contest them. This is an issue that I don't know has ever been before a Trial Chamber in this Tribunal. And I stress the following words so that the two accused hear this: It is fairly common from where I come from. You can even enter a plea of nolo contendere, which means you are not making any kind of admission and where it might be very difficult to make an --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, Ms. Korner, because you're causing problems for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's the last thing I want to do. I haven't got my headphones on. It's always more difficult when you're reading from a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't have mine on either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'll go back, because I do think this is important that the accused hear this. "It is one thing to say we admit all the facts alleged with regard to what happened in the camp at Omarska and another thing to say we simply do not contest them. That is an issue that I do not -- that I don't know has ever been before a Trial Chamber in this Tribunal. It's fairly common where I come from. You can even enter a plea of nolo contendere, which means you're not making any kind of admission and where it might be very difficult to make an admission of facts, it's quite easy to do, to simply say, "I do not contest these facts for the purposes of this trial." And it seems to me that accomplishes the same thing. It takes the Prosecutor off the hook in terms of having to prove them. So I'd like you to consider whether you would accept that kind of an agreement, representation." Your response, Judge Agius, was to say that you would discuss with your co-Judges, and then said: "Certainly I can assure you of something, that this Trial Chamber is very clear about or hasn't got any doubts about, that is the fact that you may be either requested, called upon, or voluntarily come forward and say, "We do not contest these facts," which will not -- I'm sorry. And say, "We do not contest these facts." And then you said this: "Which will not at any time then or afterwards be taken to mean, first, that your clients knew that those events were taking place or that they personally accept the fact that they are not being contested to be in any way used against them or to be prejudicial to them." And you repeated it. You gave an example with Omarska and said: "We do not -- the words 'we do not contest that that happened' doesn't mean to say that they are agreeing, that they knew about those events at the time that they were happening or that they had some or some sort of control over the situation." And you further repeated it again later. Your Honour, the matter came up again when the witness who was called quite recently on the 11th of April, BT12, and Mr. Ackerman in terms stood up, as Madam Fauveau had said by letter, that there was no contest as to the killing that had taken place. Your Honour, this is not a process by which either accused through their counsel agreeing not to contest facts in any way admits guilt, and Your Honours have made that absolutely clear that you would not in any way treat it as such. It is not helping the Prosecution. The Prosecution is perfectly willing to go on calling witnesses for as long as it takes to prove the matters alleged in the indictment in relation to the crimes that we say obviously were committed by people directly other than these two accused. It is an attempt by the Trial Chamber and by responsible counsel to make sure that the evidence that is heard live is specifically related to matters that are specifically in issue or specifically relate to the culpability of the two accused. Mr. Von Hebel in the last conference with him, made it clear one of the reasons why the Trial Chamber is so concerned is that there are other people waiting in the Detention Unit for trial who have been waiting almost as long, some of them, as Mr. Brdjanin. And unless there can be some agreement reached, this trial will go on, as I said to Your Honours when you asked me yesterday, how long in the event that we were dropping some matters this would take. And unless realistically, unless some sort of agreement can be reached, it will take -- it will clearly take the best part of two years as it is, and it will take longer. And I'm not sure how conducive that is to either accused to have to sit through a trial for two years. Your Honour, it seems to me if the reflection is taken by the accused because really this is their decision. Counsel can advise them and say, "This is what we advise you to do," but it's their decision because they're the people who this effects -- that what happened with this list of potentially agree facts was that somebody didn't really apply their mind properly to what could be agreed, that it was an attempt on behalf of Your Honours to manage this trial properly, and that in no sense does it reflect any decision or even the beginnings of a decision taken by Your Honours on the facts. And I would merely ask, that before we take the further steps that such a motion will require, reflection is given to whether this motion should be pursued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't plan to make a long speech or a large reply to what Ms. Korner had just said, because I think the moment does not permit that. I will say this: I fully accept Your Honours' statement that none of you were aware of this document. The problem is that the document says the Chamber has drafted such a list. Now, I can only understand that to be Your Honours, or that it was drafted with the specific understanding and direction of Your Honours. I would ask that you apply to yourselves, Your Honours, the same standards you apply to the detainee -- to the accused in this case, that is, if you didn't know about it, you should have. And I'm satisfied that had you known about it, it wouldn't have come out and been released and confronted me with the need to try to explain it to my client. I could spend the next year trying to explain this to Mr. Brdjanin. And this is not -- that this is not some indication by Your Honours that you believe these facts are so well established that we shouldn't further contest them. I don't know how I can ever get him to understand that. A statement that Radoslav Brdjanin was president of the ARK Crisis Staff from 5 May 1992 onwards is totally unacceptable. What does onwards mean? How long is that? Is that up until today? We all know that the Crisis Staff functioned for a very short period of time. And it's -- it is a shocking document. That's all I can say to you. I didn't sleep last night because of this, at all, and I couldn't sleep last night because of this at all. And this motion was not filed lightly. This was a very, very, very difficult position for me to get myself to, and I didn't do it precipitously or lightly. I sought the advice of many, many people whom I trust a great deal. And I can tell Your Honours that each person to whom I consulted with regard to this matter, without any prompting by me, looked at this document and said, "That is outrageous. That is a shocking outrage." And I still believe it is, and I believe it would not be here if Your Honours had any sense of what was happening behind the scenes. It's sad that this has happened. I don't -- I didn't want this to happen. I didn't ask for this to happen. The business of whether or not admissions are made with regard to facts, it seems to me, is a business between the Prosecution and the Defence. Judges, it seems to me, are to sit as impartial arbiters of the facts that they hear. I think I probably should say no more about it, but that's -- that's how I feel as I stand before you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further statements? Madame Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I fully accept your statement, but I also fully associate myself with the statement made by Mr. Ackerman. I will be very brief. I also accept what Ms. Korner has said. It is quite permissible for the Prosecutor to ask us to admit certain facts. It is quite normal for us to admit certain facts. It is also true that the admission of certain facts does not signify the culpability of our clients, above all mine. Unfortunately in this document, a sentence shocked me deeply, which we are discussing for almost three years, that is, my client's participation in the Crisis Staff. This is not a precise fact. It is not a distantly removed fact. It affects the very core of General Talic's position. I don't know where this document comes from, but I do believe that it doesn't come from you. But according to this document, it is the Chamber that drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to add something else, in the light of it. It seems to me that neither Mr. Ackerman nor Madam Fauveau are really listening to what has been said. As I say, this is the accused's decision in the end. Counsel can advise, but they have the right to make the decision. And I would earnestly ask them to consider this position. The other thing that we should make absolutely clear is however inadequately these were drafted -- and I'm sorry to say it is inadequate -- the simple answer would have been for either Defence counsel effectively to say, perhaps more parliamentary language, but, "Don't be ridiculous. Of course we're not going to agree to facts like General Talic was a member of the Crisis Staff or that Brdjanin was president of the ARK Crisis Staff from the 5th of May, 1992 onwards." Evidentially it's already known. We've already led evidence to some extent of the documents of the winding up. And I do feel that using the sort of hyperbole about not being able to sleep and shocking isn't very helpful. Your Honour, having said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I have 25 years experience on the Bench. So nothing impresses me much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the real question is I don't know from the sound of it whether either Defence counsel proposes to discuss the matter again with their clients. If they don't, well, then we have to decide where we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to Defence counsel. It's certainly not going to be discussed with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's why we've said what we needed to say, and that's it. However, I do want to make one thing clear, that one thing I would take objection to definitely, is if you receive a document for discussion, whatever meeting it would be, informal like the one which was planned for this morning, purporting to present to you matters for discussion, being presented by our legal staff. Our legal staff, vis-a-vis you, have no standing. I would object if our legal staff were to present you with a document saying, "This is what in our opinion ought to be discussed." So I see nothing strange at all if anyone did put in the document itself "the Chamber." The thing is that -- in reality, in such circumstances, seeing -- reading the Chamber has drafted this, one would stop before jumping where one should be very careful. One would stop and confirm first whether the Chamber itself had drafted this, because if that would have been the case, I would have discussed nothing further in that meeting, come straight here, and put the question to the Chamber. "Did you draft this? Are you seriously expecting us to agree to this?" That's how I would have acted. But anyway, things are what they are, and I suppose we don't need to discuss the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, the difficulty though is where we go from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The difficulty is going -- it's going to be decided by whoever is by the rules entrusted with the task of deciding such a motion. I mean, we have got nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I note Judge Schomburg's order that the trial should continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And God forbid that he hadn't ordered such a thing, because we could have the situation arising every -- every week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the expectation that we stop the proceedings in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then Your Honours, may I raise then -- the only other thing, then, if Your Honours propose to continue with the evidence this afternoon is this -- and I need to make it clear in open court. The motion request a hearing -- and can I just check the rule that's referred to -- yes -- that the hearing tomorrow at 9.30 be in the Judge's private room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's in Judge Schomburg's room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Under I -- now there are two thing -- I'm sorry. Rule 65 ter(I). That rule refers to the Pre-Trial Judge performing functions in his room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But you see that with Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But I need to make it clear to Your Honours now so that it can be passed to Judge Schomburg -- or rather, so that we can all reach agreement at least on this, that it is our joint opinion, all counsel, that if there is to be any hearing on this matter, it's an open, public motion. It must be done in open proceedings with full recording taking place. I just need to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will pass on the motion to Judge Schomburg. With the understanding, that this is all I will tell him because otherwise I cannot discuss obviously -- I am precluded from discussing any -- anything with him on the matter, except that I expect to be consulted by the rule, which I am sure that will be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, if there's nothing else, I'll ask for Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when is -- Mr. Von Hebel, Judge Schomburg is sitting this afternoon. And what time is he expected to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I'll pass on the message to Judge Schomburg. In the meantime, I think we can start. One other thing: We will need to stop at 6.00 today, rather than 6.30, because I've got something urgent to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, the break will be when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I will be regulated by Madam Registrar on that. Will you please organise this and tell me when we should be taking the break. However, if Judge Schomburg takes a break, say, in 15 minutes' time, I would prefer rather to have a short break then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you want to break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what time Judge Schomburg is having his break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think -- Your Honour, I think he's rising in -- they're doing the hour and a half. So I think around quarter to 4.00 he has a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can start and then break in 15 minutes' time. Incidentally, Madam Registrar, please, we are giving instructions directing that the first part of the transcript in which our statement -- joint statement is recorded be copied and given to Judge Schomburg, please, as Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber II. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Judge, and welcome back to the Tribunal. My apologies to you for keeping you waiting for so long, but this is a case which I sincerely wish you'll never have the like of. And we had a legal problem to attend to, and that has kept us occupied this last hour or so. So my apologies once more. I'm sure that as a judge you will understand each case has got its own problems. Could I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration once more, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, yesterday when we adjourned, you had just dealt with the fact that you had been arrested and were taken to the SUP and were beaten outside that. Now, at the police station, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the public security station Sanski Most, I was led through the main entrance into the hallway. I stayed there briefly. I was searched in the hallway. They took off my shoelaces and my belt from my trousers, and then they led me along the corridor to the back door where there are garages and prison cells. They took me to a prison -- a cell in the building within the compound behind the public security station, or the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you were put into the cell, how many people were there already?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put me in cell number one. There were four men there already when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And thereafter, did four more arrive who were placed into the same cell?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were nine of us in all in that cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Roughly, how big was that cell?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cell was 2 metres wide and about 2 and a half metres long.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to lie down at all, the nine of you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not able to lie down. We had to be in a group and in a sitting position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there a window?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cell was almost armoured, one can say. There was a small window, which wasn't open, and which was covered with steel sheeting. So this sheet of tin fully covered the window. And on that sheet -- steel sheet, there was several holes made with nails. The door was metal, made of metal, so there was no air at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the weather like in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in prison, it was rainy and temperatures changed during the day. There would be periods of sunshine, but it was heavy kind of weather.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a result of the lack of air and the number of people in the room, what happened to the cell itself, the walls?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The walls had turned dark from the humidity. There was drops of water on the walls, and our bodies were wet with perspiration, and the walls had gone almost black. And when I was put into that cell, they were yellowish in colour. And later on, they turned almost black. And down the steel sheet that was on the window, this small window, there was also sheeting on the radiator, and it was wet. There was water dripping from the body heat that was evaporating. For hours I would stand next to this sheet of steel, next to this little hole, so as to be able to breathe. Otherwise, there was no way we could manage. The same applied to the other people who were detained in that cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were you taken from the cell to be interrogated on about three or four occasions? Perhaps you could just answer "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were taken for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the people who interrogated you, did you know them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from where did they come? In other words, were they police, military, ordinary members of the public?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the interrogators, all of them who were there. They were members of the crime department of the police. Then there were members of the reserve force of the state security service attached to the army. Then from -- people from the state security of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What were they interrogating you about?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had questions prepared in advance which we had to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated on your own or together with other people, other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken from the cell alone for interrogation. But usually there would be two inspectors, and they took turns. And that is how they led the others too, individually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say they had a prepared questionnaire. Can you just summarise what they were asking you about.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They interrogated me two or three times in the police station, and they questioned me about the referendum. For instance, then why I had organised the referendum, why I had been against the Yugoslav People's Army, why I had attended meetings, certain meetings of the SDA party. They asked me about weapons. Actually, I was shocked by these questions because I had been accused in advance of having weapons, and actually I had no weapons except for an official pistol. And they asked me about automatic rifles, 20 or 30 of them. I don't remember any more. They accused me of having found weapons in my house, that they had found a light machine-gun, two Schmeissers, about three and a half thousand bullets for the machine-gun, that they had found trenches dug around my house, which was not true. Actually, I realised that I was condemned to death in advance. Simply, I had nothing to say. And the inspector who was interrogating me, his name was Branko Sobot, somebody I had worked with had the work, because he was in the crime department. And he went with me to carry out investigations. We cooperated at work. And I said to him, "But Branko, you know me, surely." Those were questions that I can remember. Of course there were others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beg your pardon. They also asked me about my family, why I had sent my wife and children to Germany. Then they asked for their address in Germany. Then they asked me about many of my neighbours, judges who had left, why I had opposed certain decisions of the Crisis Staff. Then they told me that I had wanted to organise Muslim police, a crime service that I had wanted to organise, why I had criticised the chief of police. They accused me of failing to really disclose terrorist activities by the chief of police and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, I can deal with the various things they were putting to you. Did you have the machine-guns, the bullets, all those things they were saying had been found? Were they -- did you have possession of them in your house? If you just answer "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that they were accusing you of wanting to organise Muslim police. Had you tried to organise a separate Muslim police force?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ever, because I had no competence in that area. I engaged in my profession. I worked in the court as a professional, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At any time were you ever charged with any offences in relation to these questions that they were asking you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the prison there, in the public security station, I expected an indictment. However, I received nothing, nothing in writing, even though the president of the Crisis Staff, Nedeljko Rasula on the second day after I was taken into custody, together with two other members of the Crisis Staff, came to the prison -- to the cell and told us that they -- we would be put on trial and that we would pay with our lives. If in the process of disarmament any Serb gets killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So he was saying that if -- during the disarming process any Serb gets killed, you would pay with your -- you would be put on trial and pay with your lives.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that we would be tried in any event. And he threatened us that we would have to pay with our lives, that -- or rather, that for every Serb killed, 100 Muslims would be killed, and that we were the ones who were in -- who were in prison that were responsible for everything. And on that day, there were 16 of us in two cells, because in the other cell was where the others were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were you ever put on trial?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You said that Rasula came with two other members of the Crisis Staff. Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And they were? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was a professor, Nemanja Tripkovic. And the other was designated as the command of the prison. Earlier on he had been a police commander, and he had retired. And then he was reactivated, and his name was Milutin Papric. He was in uniform -- in a blue uniform with rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just go back to the first one. What did you say his surname was? Nemanja ...?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tripkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During the course of these interrogations, was any kind of violence used against you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only against me, but against all of us, when we were taken out individually one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just deal with what happened to you. I'm simply -- at this stage during the questioning that you talked about, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, when they were taking me out, the interrogators left the room I was in. Then a young man came in, whom I didn't know, and he beat me on the soles of my feet with a pole on my soles. Then there were insults held and then he left, and then the interrogators came back. I think on one other occasion or maybe on two occasions I was beaten outside in the compound between the building and the prison. Once I was going to fetch water to carry it into the cell, and the water was in a tank next to the building some 30 or 50 metres from the prison. And there I was also hit with a wooden stick, a baseball bat in the rib area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally just before we have the break, did the person who hit you with the baseball bat, what was he? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man I think was cleaning the Mahala, because he wore black gloves with the fingers cut off. He wore glasses, and he was in uniform. I think his name is Stupar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry to stop you, but was that -- was he a policeman or a military -- an ordinary policeman, military police, or ordinary military?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from the military. I don't know whether he was a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that then -- I understand -- we've had a message to say Judge Schomburg has risen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We'll break for half an hour, resuming at 4.15 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break for half an hour, and we'll resume at 4.15. Then we'll go straight until 6.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to report two things to Your Honours. It appears that the problem that I raised yesterday with regard to Witness 207 has been solved. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness 207?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we've solved that. The Prosecution has very kindly supplied us with a list of the parts that were not to be sent for translation. I think that's solved it. The second thing, in consultation with Madam Fauveau, we are -- we will advise Judge Schomburg and we're advising this Chamber now that we are withdrawing that portion of our motion that objects to this Trial Chamber sitting during the pendency of the motion. And as far as we're concerned, we can continue to sit through all the scheduled days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. In the meantime, I would like you to know that as per your suggestion, I did in the presence of -- or together with the other two Judges and in the presence of the senior legal officer pass on the message to Judge Schomburg, the message that you asked me to pass on. And I suppose I am not a bearer of any response in the sense not officially, but I suppose if you don't hear anything, you're supposed to take the decision as it stands for the time being. Anyway, that's -- but I'm not a bearer of any response or answer or reply or information to you. So again, Judge --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- just before we go back to the Judge's evidence, I just want to be absolutely clear that in our joint view, it's inappropriate and it's not in accordance with the rules. I think that should the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I suppose, Ms. Korner, you're -- I am not exactly the right person to be addressed on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you ought to turn up as instructed, unless there is a counter-order, and explain your position at the appropriate moment to the appropriate person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The only reason I'm continuing on this is because effectively, unless a Court is arranged for tomorrow morning, there will be -- and Judge Schomburg accepts that this matter has to be raised in open court because it's an open motion and dealt with in open court, there will not be a court tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But since there is the withdrawal now of the objection for the proceedings to continue, that's not going to change much, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be preferable, I think, if this matter were to be dealt with as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As expeditiously as possible. I mean, I would have -- I better not say anything. I mean, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's not in my hands, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think it is being dealt with the utmost urgency and most attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But not in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's not up to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. That, Your Honour, I'm only saying it. I know that Your Honours effectively the legal staff that Your Honours have meet and discuss these matters. The registry hear what is I'm saying, and I just want to make that clear. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of the diary, I think Your Honour should know that we did in the interests of efficiency and harmony go through the diary again. It was done in fact, I should add, by Ms. Gustin in her spare time while Mr. Ackerman was unable to sleep at night, Ms. Gustin was unable to sleep because she was working at night. So I think I ought to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You give her a day off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She had that the other day, when Ms. Sutherland was here. And finally, Your Honour, just one other matter. I meant to mention it because it's perhaps important given the concern that these proceedings are heard in open forum. Someone yesterday spoke to me and said they were unable to attend yesterday to watch this trial, which is what they wished to do, because they were told by the security that we were in closed session. I think it's important, I mention it to Your Honours, so that it can be heard that we had a lot in closed session, through necessity, but for a member of the public to be told that it was in closed session when it was in fact in open session is not very helpful, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not very helpful. At the same time, I think at least from this side, I have a better view than you have. But we did have some spectators yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was an audience, for sure. And I actually recognised at least one person amongst the audience today that was here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I could recognise also the others. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I don't see why some were admitted and some weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. Your Honour, that's problem. I think there should be at least the security should get together and decide whether they're all going to say one thing or they're all going to say different things. But I'm simply raising that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, and I'll try to pass on the message via the registrar to the Chief of Security. I thank you. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Yes, please now proceed with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, we'd just dealt with the beatings that had occurred whilst you were in the yard and during the interrogation. Did -- were you beaten anywhere else or on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was beaten in Manjaca in the camp, that is, when I arrived up there. I will tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. I still want to deal with the police station. Anywhere else at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of the people in your cell, you described that there were four people originally and then a further four were brought in. Did the cell remain with nine people, or eventually was it reduced?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that I was brought on the 25th of May. And on that day, I found four. So together, there were five in the cell. The following day or perhaps in the following two days, another four people were brought to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they remain there until you were transported to Manjaca? Were you always nine people after that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was transferred to Manjaca -- and I was transfer there on the 17th of June -- so I was there for 24 days in that cell. Before me, a group of five persons were taken out, and they were never returned to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 12th of June. I think it was the 12th of June or perhaps the 6th of June. But in any case, two weeks before I left the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the four people who remained -- who remained with you in the cell, can you name them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. So I was there, and there was Mr. Suad Sabic, Mr. Faik Biscevic, and Mr. Ismet Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These people that you've named, can you just tell us what their positions were before they were put in the cell with you. What did Mr. Suad Sabic do?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sabic was a lawyer by training. And politically he was active, and he was a deputy in the Sanski Most municipality on behalf of the SDA party. He was in the main board of the SDA party in Sarajevo. And he was in the municipality board of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Faik Biscevic, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Faik Biscevic was a -- working in the health service. He was a dentist. And he was also a deputy in the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly on behalf of the SDA party. And for a while, I believed that he was the vice-president of the SDA party in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. What about Mr. Ismet Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ismet Jakupovic was a director of an insurance company called Dunav in Sanski Most. I think that he was a member of the reform party, a political party of the Reform forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you also detained at some stage with Mr. Catic, Stipo?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stipo Catic. Mr. Stipo Catic was also -- this is a group that I mentioned, the first five who were taken out from our cell. He was among the first five. And he was a Croat. He worked at Jugobanka, and he was a member of the Reform party, an opposition party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Fikret Saletovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Saletovic is a teacher. And he was a party of the Reform party -- an opposition party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was he also in your cell at some stage?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Exactly on the 25th of May, he was also arrested. And I found him in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- apart from the people who you -- were in your cell, did you also come to know who else had been arrested and was in the cells?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In another cell, there was Mr. Mirzet Karabeg, president of the executive council of the municipality. And then there was also Mr. Redzo Kurbegovic. He was then the elected president of the SDA party. There was also Hase Osmancevic, who was a private businessman. And he was the president of Merhamet. Then there was also Nedzad Muhic, who was the president of the misdemeanours court of the municipality. And then there was Sevdaga Hukanovic, who was underage. He was about 17 years old. He came from the locality of Vrhpolje. Then there was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Don't worry about naming more. Just generally, you've described the various positions that people held. Of the prisoners that you came across in the police station, were most of them -- or what proportion of them, people of some standing in the community, Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were all prominent people who held certain positions in the community life in Sanski Most, apart from the young man, the minor, who was brought from Vrhpolje because he had -- he had worked for a -- another young man about whom they believed that he was a member of the Green Berets in Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, whilst you were at the police station in the cells, did you hear anything or see anything to do with the attack that took place on Mahala, in area in which you lived?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, that is, the following day after -- the day after I was arrested, in the evening at around 2100 hours I heard shelling. I heard shells being fired. It was terrible because the firing of shells lasted throughout the night. They were fired almost every minute or every two to three minutes. We did not know where the shells were going to, but I felt that they were either being fired from the roof of the prison or from the football field Podgrmec, which is located right behind the building, or in front of Betonirka, which is in the immediate vicinity of the prison cells. These were terrible detonations. And at first I counted them. I counted the explosions. There were about 400 of them. And then I stopped counting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you, please -- ask you to look at again the plan of Sanski Most itself with the photographs around it, which is P475 -- 74 -- thank you. 757.1. You told us that it sounded as though they were being fired from the roof of the prison or from the football field behind the cells. Just looking at the map for a moment -- I think the best thing is if you could put it on the ELMO and just indicate when you say football fields, what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the location where the football field is, called Podgrmec, here. Right next to the edge of the field is a concrete wall, fence. And there there's the police station, and behind this concrete fence is the -- are the prison cells.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as we can see, the area called Mahala was directly across the river.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't yet know where the shells were going to. We were only able to guess in the prison in that horrifying fear. It was only in the morning at 5.00 when the policemen opened the door of the cell. They then said that Mahala was being shelled. I will then show where Mahala is. This is locality of Mahala. Here is Muhici and Otoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can -- we can take that map away. And remove the -- because I think the other is distracted to the witness. So please turn it off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what you heard during the night. Did there come a time when you would --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what you heard during the night. Did there come a time when you would -- you and others were taken from your cells and taken to watch what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the following day, that is, on the 27th of May, in the afternoon they came. They unlocked the door, and they forced us out of the cell. It was a large group of policemen. They were reservists, and there were also soldiers who had been in Mahala. They led us out to watch Mahala burning, to watch Mahala on fire. And smoke -- I saw black clouds, the whole sky filled with them on the southern side. It was on fire. At that point I saw that Mahala was burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The soldiers you described who had been in Mahala, first what kind of soldiers? From -- were you able to tell from which unit?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the 6th Krajina Brigade and members of the Serb Territorial Defence. And I knew all these people who were members, and they were also members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come back to that in a moment?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just stop there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you know that they'd been in Mahala? Did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had already said. At 5.00 in the morning on the 27th of May, a policeman came who unlocked the door. And he was armed. And then he was followed by several others, and he said that that night they had attacked Mahala, and that's when I found out. In fact, he was very frustrated and angry, and he threatened us that we would pay for this. He said some things like, for instance, that 1.000 people had been killed and that there were 400 Green Berets left who hadn't surrendered yet. But in the course of the day, we would certainly overwhelm them and kill them. These were terrifying things. And of course I was in a state of shock, and I didn't believe this. I knew that there had been no resistance whatsoever in Mahala. I even then knew that this was propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. What I actually meant was: How did you know that those soldiers and the SOS who took you out, those particular soldiers and those particular members of the SOS, had taken part in the action against Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they themselves said it. They said that they had been in Mahala and that they had destroyed the mosque. And they said that there were snipers who were firing from my house and that Bosko Banjac, who was a former friend of mine, a teacher, that he had called by telephone and that he had asked a cannon called Crni Djordje or Black Djordje, and that he had called Dusan Saovic, known as Njunja, to come with the cannon and neutralise the attack from my house. And I said, "Well, there is nobody in my house." And I pulled a key out of my pocket, a key to my house. And I said, "My wife and children are in Germany. There is no one there." They then said, "We had to set it on fire." I was told this by Bosko Banjac, this friend of mine, and Nemanja Tripkovic and another soldier who's a neighbour of mine, a Serb from Kljucka Street - Kljucka - who said that they had been on my street and the house was set on fire. And the others told me as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that Mr. Tripkovic was a member of the Crisis Staff and came to see you in your cells. Were there any other people there who you knew then or later found out were members of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Nemanja Tripkovic was together with Rasula. So two of them from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Rasula was one of the people who took you out to watch your house and Mahala burning.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rasula wasn't there then. He was with Tripkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And they came --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And on the 26th, I said earlier that was on the 26th in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. But are you saying -- we need to get this clear. Are you saying that the time you were taken out of the cell to watch Mahala burn, Mr. Tripkovic was there. Or was this the incident when he visited you in your cell?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tripkovic was in an army uniform then. And Bosko Banjac was also in an army uniform. And they had just arrived then at that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But did they -- are they two of the people who were outside with you when you were watching Mahala burn?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, whilst that was happening, did anything else happen to you and the other prisoners who were outside?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That very same evening, Tomo Delic came, who was a duke, a Vojvoda. He brought a bottle of brandy, and he made us drink this brandy in all this horror. They didn't let us return to the cell immediately. An incident could have occurred between the police and the army. We had to drink alcohol in all that horror. On that occasion, Tomo Delic told me, "You were in a census commission of the municipality of Sanski Most. Why didn't you register, record the victims from the Second World War that the Serbs had suffered or who were in Susnjar?" I said that I was not a member of the census commission. He then said that we would all pay and that they would balance the figures out, the number of people who had been killed in the Second World War, and that we would pay for Susnjar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. -- And Tomo Delic was who? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomo Delic, as far as I know, was formationally appointed to be an SOS commander. He was in fact also in the 4th Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade. He was one of the main people who provided finances for the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And just so that it becomes entirely clear, apart from the obvious that you were watching your homes burn, what was the point of making you drink brandy? Why was that so terrible?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above all, you know that we are Muslims. Furthermore, in that horror in the most difficult moment of our existence, we were being made to drink --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he can -- you can move to the next question, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just don't want to take it for granted that everybody had understood why that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You remained, you told us, at the police station until the 17th of June, when you were transported. Before you were transported, were there earlier convoys of prisoners taken to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know in prison what was going on outside. I've already said that four of the prisoners from our cell were taken away. We didn't know where they went. Also from another cell they had taken some people. We knew that there were, I think, also four people left there. But an engineer came to the cell, Muhamed Arapovic, who used to work in the municipality as a construction inspector. And this was on the 27th of May. He said that on the radio they had said -- they had accused him of being a sniper and of firing from his building with a sniper rifle, whereas in fact he was at his parents' place in another street, and he came of his own accord to report to the police. And then he said to us that across the bridge -- when he was crossing the bridge -- he saw snipers who were firing from a room in the Sanus Hotel. They were soldiers of the 6th Krajina Brigade who had been positioned there earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he said that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Unless this is particularly relevant to the question of going to Manjaca, I want to deal with the convoys to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to add that he told us that Dr. Alagic Mehmed had been killed in front of the department store. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay can I tell you, sir that, there are going to be a lot of people that are going to be dealing with a lot of the events that you can cover. The convoys to Manjaca, perhaps we can just deal with those -- was the first convoy of prisoners on the 6th of June from which some of your cellmates were sent -- on which.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently discover from conversations and/or investigations that six people had been removed from that first transport to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I learnt that at Manjaca, that six persons had been returned. And we never found them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then was the second transport on or about the 11th of 12th of June?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, were six people removed from that convoy who have never been seen again?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I learnt this at Manjaca, straight away from the detainees who were in that convoy. The names of the people -- and there were six of them -- who were in that convoy -- or rather, in the truck who were turned back and whom we never found.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, were you sent on the 3rd convoy from the prison to Manjaca on the 17th of June, as you've told us?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in that convoy in a truck on the 17th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me just a moment. Your Honours, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, may I make an announcement. I have just been asked by Judge Schomburg to convey to you the following notice: Namely, that upon your request, the hearing on a motion will take place in a courtroom available, either I or III -- and I'm being told it's I now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At 9.30 a.m. In public session in the presence of that accused. To that extent, his former order of today is hereby vacated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour for letting us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Just to make sure that you are prepared for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, what I want you to look at now is a video, which you've had a chance to see before we move to Manjaca of the Sanski Most area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, which we did look at right at the beginning. But I want to witness to identify the various areas. It's being handed to the audiovisual unit. I think the usher needs to put the television on video evidence. And I hope it's actually cued to the to the same place. I honestly can't remember what the exhibit number of that is. Yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You've seen this before. Can you just tell us what's the camera looking at at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a very blurred picture. I mean, I would be very surprised if the witness can tell us --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've been through this with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's on pause at the moment. Can you tell us what this is, sir, what we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in Prijedor, Carakovo, the bridge at Carakovo, I think. That's better. Now, this is Sanski Most, the Krings hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Will you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you -- what we're looking at there, you say, sir, is that the long building with the white sort of roof?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The narrow one, long and narrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's the Krings factory?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has a white roof. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the sports hall there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we -- I'm sorry. Could we pause -- go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The sports hall where?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Run it forward again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forward, please. Now. Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. The sports hall is which one? Where we can see the field?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right to the left, to the extreme left, down, with the red roof. That is the city sports hall. Before that we saw the Krings hall, where people were detained on that day when Sanski Most was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also, this sports hall was used to detain people from Mahala, from Otoke, and Muhici on the 27th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move on then, please, with the movie.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we pause there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back. Can we go back. Just for a moment. One shot. Oh, that will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will do. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Mahala district of the town to the left from the department store, the mosque is at the very entrance to the Mahala area. The Mahala neighbourhood is on the left bank of the Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to that mosque? I mean, this is obviously taken last year. But during this period.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a new mosque that was built after 1997, 1998. There used to be a mosque there which was destroyed by the armed forces of the 6th Krajina Brigade. For the first time on the 27th of May, they tried to destroy it with explosives. It was destroyed in three stages and totally destroyed, and the material was completely removed so that the area was turned into a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to deal with the question, then, please, of mosques and other religious buildings. How many mosques did Sanski Most have in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Sanski Most municipality, there was a total of 27 mosques. They were all completely destroyed, as well as four Catholic churches.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the town of Sanski Most itself, how many mosques were there? Just the one or more than one?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only had one town mosque, the Hamzibegova mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Catholic churches? Any in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We also had one Catholic church, which is situated in Banja Luka Street in the immediate vicinity of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just -- yes. If we go on. We're looking there at the entrance to -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Hang on. Just pause for a moment, please. Can we go back again. Thank you. To the bridge. Stop. Okay. Stop it there, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the bridge. On the other side of the bridge is that correct where the Hotel Sanus was?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sanus Hotel is situated to the right of the river -- to the right-hand side of the bridge. As soon as you cross the bridge, it's on the right-hand side. And on the left-hand side is the department store, Sanjaka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry. If we'd like to go on the with film.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop here, please. On the right-hand side, in the right-hand corner is the elementary school called Hasan Kikic. People were detained there too: Men, Muslim men, and Croat men, citizens of Sanski Most municipality, to the right, behind the school in a hall, and they mistreated them there too. And from this school they drove them to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could move the film on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. Here you can see the Serbian Orthodox church in the middle, which is completely intact and was intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could you move the film.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're now looking at Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can move forward a little to -- so that we can see the garages where people were detained and mistreated. So will you wind forward a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move the film.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. Right at the bottom in the left-hand corner we can see three doors. These were concrete garages where on the 26th, that is, on the eve of the attack and on the 27th and onwards, they would detain people there, mostly Bosniaks, and Croats. In those three garages, about 150 people were detained. They were very badly tortured there and beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. Don't worry. We're going to hear from witnesses about that. Just so that we -- I think we may get another shot of it in a moment but where was the police station in relation to those garages that you just indicated?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little forward, please. Can you move the film forward, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wind back a little, please. [In English] Stop. Stop. [Interpretation] The police station is situated on the left-hand side above the middle of the screen. You can see that it consists of two parts. The actual prison premises are next to the wall, or rather, to the far left towards the football pitch. And you can see a grey surface. That is the prison. And next to the prison, parallel with the building, is the ammunition warehouse where ammunition and materiel were held. And that is also where the command of the Territorial Defence staff was and the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, which was removed when the attack started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
