utterances.text: It was relocated into the hills.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's also -- is it the football field that you were talking about at the back that we can just see on the left of the picture? And I think we get another shot of --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move the film on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you can see -- Stop, please. A little back. A little backwards, please. Stop now. Now you can see the tallest building was the building of the Serbian Territorial Defence. That is also where the radio station was relocated to. And then next to it is the police. And in the ground -- on the ground floor, there's a hall. And the prison, as I have already explained, is this lower building facing the football field. And the higher building is where the weapons and equipment was kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we can move the film.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just waiting, because I think there's one other part. We're going out of Sanski Most now. All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before we -- if we just pause for a moment -- which direction is this showing now, Judge, if you can remember? If you know, I should say, not if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is moving in the direction towards Tomina and Vrhpolje Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps -- yes, I thought --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we just run it a little long. I think it takes just about a minute or so. Could we run the film a little longer. I think you're able to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Tomina, the settlement of Tomina. This is the main road going from Sanski Most towards Kljuc. To the right and left of the road is the settlement of Tomina. At the end of this road, there should be a bridge across the Sana River in the settlement of Vrhpolje, where crimes were committed. That's the bridge I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we pause it there for a moment. Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going hear later that you were present when exhumations were conducted at the bridge. Where were the graves found?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to say one sentence only. This road to the left is the road along which we were driven to Manjaca. So from this crossroads. And in answer to your question, this is a new bridge that was built after the war. The old bridge was destroyed in 1995 in September by the Serb armed forces. Below that bridge, which resembled this one that we see now, we discovered and exhumed two mass graves of killed civilians from the area of Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, and Kljevci. One mass grave was found and exhumed on the right-hand side, directly below the bridge. A second mass grave was discovered to the left of the bridge, on the left-hand side below the bridge. A third mass grave in that location was found downstream, about 150 metres from the bridge on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can stop the film now. Your Honour, I'm helpfully told by Ms. Gustin, as ever, that it's Exhibit P447 that we've been watching, so the transcript reflects it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, I want to come now to Manjaca. You were taken there on the 17th of June. How many people were taken there with you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was a lorry at that time, and I was led out of the cell and so was Mr. Ismet Jakupovic, and there was a lorry waiting in front of Betonirka. They called out my name, and this was done by my former colleague, Drago Vujinic, who had worked in SUP. And he had lists of names. When we went out of the cell, he told me to bend my head down and to put my hands behind my back. I was escorted by two armed soldiers and another two armed soldiers were escorting Mr. Ismet Jakupovic. When we went through the corridor and went out of the police building there were cordons of policemen, soldiers, civilians. It was terrible. They took us 150 metres away to the compound of Betonirka. And I asked Drago, "Where are you taking us?" He replied, "You'll see." When we got to the lorry, he ordered us to board the lorry. There were 22 or 23 Bosniaks in the lorry. In any case, these were all people who I knew. They were either intellectuals or private entrepreneurs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or they were --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Or they were ...?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all people known to me, prominent citizens of Sanski Most and the surrounding locations around Sanski Most. There were 23 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any of these people in any kind of military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one. Absolutely nobody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had anybody been charged or tried for -- sorry. Had anybody been charged with any criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one had been charged. That means nobody received an indictment, charges in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had any of these people, as far as you knew, been involved in any kind of fighting or resistance to the Serbs, the SDS, the 6th Krajina Brigade, the SOS?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you were taken to Manjaca. And I want to deal with what happened when you arrived at Manjaca. But had you -- did you know about Manjaca before this? Had you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, when I came in the lorry and I saw there were people with injuries on their faces, that they had been beaten up on their bodies, and when the vehicle set off and the canvas sheeting came down, we then said, "Would we be killed? Where are we being taken?" Nobody knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You misunderstood, sir. It's my fault. Had you heard of Manjaca as either a military training ground or some kind of military prison camp before your arrival there? Not in the back of the lorry, but I mean before you were arrested even.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I knew quite a lot about Manjaca because Manjaca was a large training ground of the JNA. It was one of the largest training grounds used for training. And this ground consisted of a large area, about 40 kilometres square. And it was situated about 30 kilometres from Banja Luka, that is, perhaps 40 or fewer kilometres from Sanski Most, between the municipalities of Banja Luka, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were driven in this truck to the camp. What happened to you when you actually arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived, they then opened the canvas cover and they started to call out the names. This was done by Drago Vujinic, who was carrying the list of names. And we started to get off. But we had already heard the army and the police there. As people were getting off the lorry, beating started, severe beating started. Each one of us who got off the lorry was immediately beaten with pre-prepared wooden poles. And when we all got off the lorry, they ordered us to put the hands behind our back, to bend our heads, not to look around. We went through a cordon of soldiers, of military policemen, who were beating us severely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, you said -- talked about the pre-prepared wooden poles. Was any -- were any other weapons used to beat you and your fellow prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they were taking us in, they were beating us with wooden poles, with electric cables, with rifle butts. They were kicking us in their boots. Each one of us was a recipient of severe beating. Once we were inside, we were then forced onto these -- this wire fence. I saw these stables, and we had to run to a stable. And as we came in, they then told us to lift our heads and to look around.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Before we go on to this, when you -- you said that the -- Drago was calling out a list of names. Was anything said by anybody when your name was called out?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he called out my name, they went for me. They said, "Here is another Draganovic." And I became even more frightened, but I presumed that there were other people with the same surname like me, my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where did most of your relatives live?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in the municipality of Kljuc. And the place is called Hadzici, that is Pudin Han. And my relatives were from there. That's where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. You told us that you were taken to the stables. What happened when you got to the stable?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, I'll have to start from the beginning. When we entered the first stable, they then showed us around to look at the people who had been brought there before us. And they said that these people were dead and that we would end up like them. And I saw people who were laid out. They had their hair cut. They were barefoot. They were lying on their fronts on the ground in one side of the stables in a -- in a box, a horse's box. There were many of them, perhaps 200. I glanced at them, and they were all lying on the ground. Their heads were -- was down. Their hands were behind their backs. That's how they were. They were like wood, pieces of wood. And then they continued to beat us. And then they took us to another stable. When we entered another stable, they again ordered us to stop and to look around, to lift our heads. And I saw the same scene. People were -- with their hair cut. They were practically naked and barefooted. They were lying with their heads down. Their faces were turned down to the ground, and their hands were up behind their backs, and they were laid out like sardines. And then they took us further. Again in a hurry while they were beating, because there were several of them on both sides of us. Then they brought us to a room for which I later -- about which I later learnt that this was a solitary cell, also a small stable. It's a small building below the stable in camp number 1. There they forced us into this small stable while beating us and ordered us to immediately lie down on the concrete floor, that we mustn't look up, that our hands had to be behind our back. They were doing all this while they were beating us, and this beating lasted almost for an hour or two hours. And then they left us like this and they went to change. In fact, the first thing they did was they searched us, and we stood up to get the money out, everything we had in our pockets. They took money from everybody. They said that if they found money on anyone, that they would kill that person. I had money, and they were sewn into my underwear. And while they were searching, I tore my underwear, and I got the money out and I put it in my hand behind my back. That's how they ordered it to be. They took the money. They took the money from everybody in this way. And they then ordered us again to lie down on the concrete floor. When they had a change of clothes, it had already been raining and they were a little wet or perhaps wet with sweat from the beating. They came again the same evening. And they continued to beat us. This cannot be described. During that first night, several occasions they came and they would be -- they were beating us up, all of us. They were beating us. They were armed with wooden poles, which were about 1 and a half metres long. They were about 5 to 10 centimetres thick. They had electric cables -- they beat us with electric cables that were about 5 centimetres thick. They were about 1 metre long. Then they had batons, different items.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there for a moment. Who was doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were military policemen in uniforms. We didn't -- we were not allowed to look while we were being beaten, but in all this beating, after the blows had fallen, we would fall down. And of course I was able to see that these were uniforms of the military police, because they had on them, white belts with the insignia of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell if there were any officers there, or was it just ordinary military policemen? Or if you can't, say. Then tell us.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Because we were not allowed to look. I -- if I can just say. Whether it was that night or perhaps the following night, after all the beatings, in the end we all had to stand. And then one by one they would then beat them to the floor with a hit -- with a blow in the back. And then the soldier who hit us would have a run, and then he would use a karate blow to the spine, and each one of us would fall on the floor. I can still feel that blow today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You were in Manjaca, I think, until December of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Until the 14th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to deal now with various aspects of life in Manjaca during that period that you were there. First of all, the beatings. You've described what happened to you that first night. Thereafter, were you beaten again?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that isolation with -- together with this group, I spent perhaps seven or eight days. I don't remember exactly. Every night -- every day we were beaten, all of us. And then they would -- they would wake us up about 2.00 or 3.00 in the evening. They would come -- several of them would come to beat us. I was then woken up twice or three times. And that beating would then last for half an hour -- 45 minutes or an hour. I don't know. There were five of them. I know that there were three military policemen. There was one soldier. He was a soldier in a camouflage uniform, and he had a helmet on his head, and he had something -- some mask on his helmet. They beat us. One was using an -- a cable to beat. Another one was using a baton. Two were using their boots, kicking us in the stomach, in the chest, in the mouth. And this young soldier, he was the worst. He was using his hands in the area of the heart, where the heart was. So the worst was that I would have to stand to attention with my hands behind my back, and he would use his hands as a boxer, beating me in the area of the heart. I would receive over 20 blows while he was doing that. And the others were beating at the same time -- were beating me at the same time. I fell several times on the floor, on the concrete, and then I would get up -- I don't know how -- because once you fall down, then they beat you even -- in an even worse way. They would be kicking with the boots. I don't know how I survived that night. It was once or twice, but the second time there were three of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Over the period of the next six months or so, were you beaten again in this sort of fashion?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went out of this solitary cell, there were several beatings. When I was in the stable on one occasion, some man -- a military policeman called Popovic, he was beating me in the face with his fists, with his hands. Several times they would call us out by name in the night; not just me, but the others as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did these beatings take place as far as you were concerned - I'll come to others in a moment - on a daily basis, a weekly basis, monthly, or was it just random?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you just mean as far as I'm concerned, I can say that after that I was beaten about another four or five times. No longer after that. But there were people who were more beaten than I was on many more occasions. There were people who were beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I'm going to ask you about those people, but I just want to concentrate on you for a moment. When did the beatings stop, then, as far as you were concerned? How long after your arrival, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in the solitary cell, we were then taken for interrogation outside of the compound to the command. And that was -- at that interrogation, there was the officer who was taking a statement, and he asked, "Were you beaten?" And I was -- I was black on my face and on my body, and I said, "No, I wasn't beaten." After that -- Could you please repeat the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand. And this is the final question. You told us you were beaten five or six times. At what period -- how long after your arrival at the camp did the beatings against you stop? Was it a week, two weeks, a month?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about 60 days there were no longer beatings in that camp and I was not beaten any more. But those first 60 days were horrible for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just one further question: What sort of -- you've described how you were black in your face and body. What sort of injuries did you suffer as a result of those beatings?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had, first of all, an injury to my spine from all the beating I received. And then I also had broken teeth, two teeth. I had injuries on my face, on my legs. I had bruises on my legs, and the circulation was weakened by this. I had injuries on the left side -- of the left kidney. I had injuries in the chestal area. These were the injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did -- I want to ask separately about medical treatment. But do you have any results still from those injuries today?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can feel that. First of all, the psychological trauma, which is present -- which has been present since then. And the trauma has manifested from time to time. I also feel injuries to my joints and constant pain in the back, in the spine when I'm breathing. When I breathe in -- when I breathe in with my lungs and then when I stop breathing, then I can feel that the air is then slowly going from the lungs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, we'll stop here for today. It will also give you a little bit of a rest. We will continue tomorrow at 2.15 in this same courtroom, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just a small correction. I was informed that for tomorrow's Motion Hearing before Judge Schomburg will be convened in Courtroom II instead of Courtroom I. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the final word on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, before it was I or III; now it's II. So we'll all meet tomorrow at 2.15 and continue with the evidence of the judge. I thank you and have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
